name: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all the value is the nuclear, pandemic and AI coverage, against risks that kill people everywhere, and the climate coverage's deaths are worldwide too, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (Chicago) publishes expert journalism on nuclear weapons, climate change, biological threats and AI on its open website and in its magazine, and sets the Doomsday Clock each January; this model covers all its programmes in the year to June 2025 ($3.5M spent). At the defaults it averts about 20 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 1.0 to 420 on the combined range: 94% of that is the nuclear coverage (about half the cost), valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of nuclear war (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts) times how far journalism applies, with deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate; the pandemic and AI coverage add 4% and 2%, and the climate coverage, valued in tonnes of CO₂e at a typical climate dollar, almost nothing. It is below the Arms Control Association because only about half its spending is on nuclear risk and journalism is further from decisions than briefs used by Congress. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; the range runs ten times either way); the result also moves with the years a cut counts and with how the spending splits between areas, which the accounts don't report. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work is measured.

rows.explainer: The climate-change coverage (its editor's beat: cuts to US climate science, wildfires, carbon sinks, solar power), the March 2025 magazine issue on environmental tipping points and the Clock statement's climate section: 15% (8% to 25%). The return reports one programme, so the areas are split by our judgment from what the Bulletin publishes: four area editors, one each for nuclear affairs, climate change, disruptive technologies and biosecurity (staff page); the magazine's 2025 issues (nuclear materials, environmental tipping points, pandemics, geopolitical flashpoints, the Trump administration and world order, and an 80th-anniversary issue across the four areas); the Doomsday Clock statement, which covers all four; the Nuclear Notebook and most of the year's most-read articles (Iran's nuclear programme, Hiroshima and Nagasaki), which are nuclear.

rows.label: Climate: tonnes of CO₂e a year a typical $1 million of climate public-interest work cuts, once in effect
rows.explainer: No shared figure exists for a typical dollar of climate work, so a ranged judgment: 1,000 tonnes a year per $1 million (100 to 10,000), anchored on our Union of Concerned Scientists climate model, whose analysis and advocacy behind five named US wins comes to about 5,600 tonnes in all per $1 million given; before that model's missing-data step (0.5) and next-dollar factor (0.33), which this model applies again in its own rows, about 34,000 tonnes, some 7,000 a year over the five years a win counts by default (its share of each win, 1% to 10%, already in). A typical climate dollar has no named win and much of it backs policies that fail, so about a seventh of that; the range runs ten times either way, as the shared cuts per dollar for the other areas. How far journalism trails campaigning work is climate_evidence_adj; whether others would have written the articles is climate_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Climate: years from the coverage to a policy it helps
rows.explainer: From the year's articles to a policy decision they help bring about: about a year, our judgment, 0 to 3, as the other branches; the policy's own wait until its tonnes are avoided is the shared figure added in climate_years_until_effect.

rows.label: Climate: years until the tonnes are avoided

rows.explainer: The shared years a cut counts ($win_years_counted), each discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Climate: tonnes of CO₂e averted (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The climate spending in millions × tonnes a year per $1 million × the discounted years they count.

rows.label: Work outside the catastrophic risks: share of the cost
rows.explainer: Coverage that bears on none of the four risks: US government efficiency and the Treasury, Big Tech's power over governance, US health politics beyond pandemics, the Mars-colonisation piece, the Arts + Science programme's concerts. It cuts no risk of a global catastrophe, so it is in no area; its value is a small share in unmodelled_benefits_adj. 10% (3% to 20%), our judgment from the annual report's list of the year's coverage.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small nuclear project applies to the Bulletin's nuclear journalism and the Clock. The Bulletin's reach is large for the field: almost seven million views of its open website in 2024 and more than 500,000 readers a month in 2025, the magazine in 7,500 libraries, and the January 2025 Doomsday Clock announcement in 5,659 news stories on the day and 456,326 page views in its first week (annual reports 2024 and 2025). But it informs rather than campaigns: its articles reach officials and researchers only through what they read, with no uptake by a government or lab named for the year. Above typical for reach and standing (eighty years, the Clock quoted by every large news outlet), below for distance from decisions: 0.7 (0.3 to 1.2), our judgment, the template's figure for typical work, below the Arms Control Association's 0.8 (research and briefs used by Congress) and FAS's Nuclear Information Project (counts governments use).

rows.label: AI field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project applies to the Bulletin's AI journalism: commentary and explainers for a general audience, much of it on AI's power over politics and the economy rather than on catastrophic failure or misuse, with no uptake by a lab or government named. Below typical: 0.5 (0.2 to 1), our judgment, below FAS's 0.7 for its AI policy proposals.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small biosecurity project applies to the Bulletin's biosecurity journalism and the Pathogens Project's reporting on risky pathogen research: expert analysis read in the field (laboratory safety, mirror life, attribution of engineered threats), part of it on US health politics further from a pandemic. 0.6 (0.25 to 1.1), our judgment, between the AI coverage's 0.5 and the nuclear coverage's 0.7.

rows.label: Climate coverage: how far the typical climate dollar applies
rows.explainer: How far the typical climate dollar of climate_tco2e_per_year_per_million (advocacy and analysis behind policy) applies to the Bulletin's climate journalism: explanatory articles in a field with many larger climate outlets, with no policy uptake named. 0.3 (0.1 to 0.7), our judgment, well below its nuclear coverage's 0.7, because the anchor is campaigning work and climate has far more of it.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: share no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Whether the nuclear journalism would have been published now by others: Arms Control Today, War on the Rocks, Outrider and the large newspapers cover nuclear weapons, but few for a general audience in such depth, and no one else sets the Clock. 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9), our judgment, the figure the Arms Control Association's, FAS's and NTI's models give the same question; that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: AI field work: share no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Whether the AI journalism would have been published now by others: AI is covered by every large outlet and by many specialist newsletters and think tanks, so much of it would be written elsewhere. 0.5 (0.2 to 0.8), our judgment, below FAS's 0.6 for AI policy work.

rows.label: Pandemic field work: share no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Whether the biosecurity journalism would have been published now by others: STAT, Science and the health press cover pandemics, but few outlets cover laboratory risk and misuse of the life sciences as a security question. 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9), our judgment, between the nuclear and AI coverage.

rows.label: Nuclear field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: The Bulletin's share of the resources behind its articles, with what others give unpaid or with their own funding. Worked, our rough count at about $75 an hour: outside experts write most of its more than 350 articles a year (about 250 at about 25 hours, $470,000); the Science and Security Board's scientists set the Clock (about 20 members, a week each, $80,000 at $100 an hour); the Federation of American Scientists writes the Nuclear Notebook in its own paid time (about six a year, $40,000, nuclear only, in FAS's own cost). About $0.59M beside $3.53M of cost: 0.86, so 0.85 (0.7 to 0.95), our judgment, for every area alike (the Notebook's part lowers the nuclear figure by about 1%). Grants the Bulletin receives are in its cost, so they lower nothing here; FAS's model credits the Notebook to FAS's spending, so no dollar's effect counts twice.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether the Bulletin's other funders (Carnegie Corporation, the Future of Life Institute, the Holthues Trust and its individual donors) would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.bulletin_of_the_atomic_scientists (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment, as for every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of the Bulletin's work is measured, on the risks (a typical project's cut and forecast chances) or on emissions (the climate branch's tonnes are judged), so the shared missing-data step applies to every branch (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled (share of the modelled value)
rows.explainer: Good beyond what is counted, each part a share of the modelled value (mostly the nuclear branch's): coverage of a single detonation or a limited nuclear war (Iran, India and Pakistan), which kills far fewer than 10% of people and has no shared forecast (nuclear_smaller_per_year 0), 8%; the work outside the four risks in other_cost_share (10% of the cost: government efficiency, technology and democracy, its harms far smaller than a catastrophe's), 1%; an eighty-year public archive that teachers, students and other writers use, 1%. 10% (0 to 30%) in all, our judgment, as the Arms Control Association's 10%.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). Journalism about AI and pathogens doesn't speed up dangerous capabilities. 0, down to −5%, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): critics say the Doomsday Clock's alarm can feed fatalism or be dismissed as crying wolf, and biosecurity articles could in principle point to a hazard; neither is shown to happen, and the Bulletin publishes no technical weapons or pathogen detail. 0, down to −5%, our judgment, as the Arms Control Association.
